content: 1. The study conducted in Bujumbura, Burundi, evaluated the effectiveness of cervical testing in detecting precancerous cervical lesions among HIV-positive women attending an HIV clinic. This cross-sectional study was published in BMJ Open in 2019. 2. The HARP study assessed the performance of careHPV testing in identifying high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) among women living with HIV-1 in Burkina Faso and South Africa. The findings were published in the International Journal of Cancer. 3. Research by Womack et al. explored HPV-based cervical cancer screening in populations at high risk for HIV infection. The study highlighted the utility of HPV testing in such high-risk groups. 4. Sahasrabuddhe et al. compared visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cervical cytology for detecting high-grade cervical neoplasia in HIV-infected women in India. The study emphasized the diagnostic accuracy of these methods. 5. Zhang et al. investigated the diversity of HPV infections among HIV-infected women in Yunnan, China, providing insights into the prevalence and types of HPV in this population. 6. De Andrade et al. identified factors associated with colposcopy-histopathology-confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia among HIV-infected women in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, highlighting the importance of histopathological confirmation. 7. Raposo et al. evaluated the performance of cytology and hybrid capture II in screening for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in HIV-positive women, emphasizing the diagnostic value of these methods. 8. Anderson et al. assessed the accuracy of the Papanicolaou (Pap) test among HIV-infected women, demonstrating its role in cervical cancer screening in this population. 9. Cohn et al. examined the role of HPV DNA assays and repeated cervical cytology in detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia among HIV-infected women, emphasizing the importance of combining diagnostic approaches. 10. Maiman et al. studied the prevalence, risk factors, and accuracy of cytologic screening for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in women with HIV, providing critical data on screening efficacy. 11. Branca et al. compared the performance of cytology and colposcopy in diagnosing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in HIV-positive and HIV-negative women, highlighting differences in diagnostic outcomes. 12. Kitchener et al. concluded that colposcopy is not always necessary to assess cervical risk in HIV-positive women, based on an international cohort study of cervical pathology. 13. Petry et al. evaluated HPV testing as a primary screening tool for cervical cancer in HIV-infected women, demonstrating its effectiveness over a multi-year period. 14. Massad et al. analyzed the negative predictive value of Pap testing in HIV-positive women, discussing implications for screening intervals in this population. 15. Harris et al. investigated the incidence of cervical squamous intraepithelial lesions in relation to HIV serostatus, CD4 cell counts, and HPV test results, providing insights into disease progression. 16. Keller et al. assessed the risk of cervical precancer and cancer in HIV-infected women with normal cervical cytology and no evidence of oncogenic HPV infection, emphasizing the importance of regular monitoring. 17. Keller et al. also studied cervical precancer risk in HIV-infected women who tested positive for oncogenic HPV despite normal Pap test results, highlighting the need for vigilant follow-up. 18. Alade et al. demonstrated that HPV co-testing effectively triages normal cervical cytology in HIV-positive women aged 30 years and older, supporting its use in this demographic. 19. Joshi et al. reported on a four-year follow-up study from India, evaluating the outcomes of cervical cancer screening in HIV-positive women, emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring. 20. Firnhaber et al. conducted a prospective one-year follow-up of HIV-infected women screened for cervical cancer using VIA, cytology, and HPV testing in Johannesburg, South Africa, highlighting the comparative effectiveness of these methods. 21. Jalil et al. explored the use of hybrid capture as a screening tool for cervical lesions in HIV-infected women in a Brazilian cohort, providing valuable insights into its diagnostic utility. 22. Debeaudrap et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on residual or recurrent precancerous lesions after treatment in HIV-infected women, emphasizing the importance of post-treatment follow-up. 23. Greene et al. compared cryotherapy and loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) for cervical disease recurrence among HIV-positive women with high-grade cervical lesions in Kenya, based on a randomized clinical trial. 24. Atemnkeng et al. reviewed the impact of antiretroviral therapy on the detection of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2+) during post-treatment follow-up in HIV-infected women, providing evidence for its role in management strategies. 25. Omeng’e et al. evaluated the use of VIA, Pap smear, and high-risk HPV testing for post-treatment cervical cancer screening in HIV-positive women, discussing the prioritization of different tests. 26. De Vuyst et al. studied residual disease and HPV persistence after cryotherapy for CIN2/3 in HIV-positive women in Kenya, highlighting the need for effective post-treatment surveillance. 27. A scoping review of follow-up strategies after screening or treatment in the general population identified gaps in evidence for optimal follow-up intervals and test selection, particularly for HIV-positive women. 28. The systematic review of primary studies revealed no direct comparisons of different follow-up periods using the same screening algorithms, underscoring the need for further research in this area. 29. Evidence from systematic reviews and modeling studies informed WHO guidelines on the use of thermal ablation and cryotherapy for cervical precancer lesions, emphasizing the relative sensitivity and specificity of different tests. 30. A scoping review of the literature on cervical cancer screening initiation and cessation ages found limited studies comparing outcomes for different age groups, leading to recommendations based on prevalence and acceptability data.
